title: Busy But Not Profitable: The Six Patterns We Keep Seeing Holding Dentists Back - Welcome to Dental Unscripted

You're Busy But Not Profitable, Here's Where the Money Is Probably Going

We hear this constantly from practice owners: "I'm slammed, I'm exhausted, but where's the money?" After doing financial reviews on hundreds of practices, here are the patterns we keep seeing.

Adding a whole day to the schedule.

This is the most common one. You're doing $800K on three days with a lean team, one doc, one hygienist, one DA, one front desk, and that math actually works. Some of the most profitable practices we've coached run exactly that setup. We have multiple clients doing $1.5M on three days out of six or seven ops.

The instinct is to add a fourth clinical day when you feel maxed out. But the minute you commit to that fourth day, your entire team's wages go up 33%. If you can't fill that day with proportional production, and most can't right away, your profit takes the hit first. Worse, your team gets accustomed to that new paycheck. Try pulling back to three days after that. Good luck.

Before you add a day, add a chair. Add a DA. That's a $25–35/hour investment that can double your throughput without touching your schedule footprint.

The benchmark: If you're not doing at least $35K per op per month, none of the "should I add a day / hire an associate / expand" discussions even apply yet. Get your existing chairs producing before you start adding complexity.

Cleaning teeth instead of doing restorative.

This one drives me nuts. You've got a startup twelve months in, three weeks booked out, crowns booked 3–4 weeks out, new patients waiting weeks to get in, and the owner won't hire a hygienist because they cost $50–60/hour.

Think about what you're actually doing. You would never take a job paying $40K when you had a $100K offer on the table. But that's exactly what you're doing when you sit in a hygiene chair producing $150/hour instead of doing restorative at $500/hour. Even if the hygiene column breaks even on wages, you've freed yourself up for the high-dollar procedures your patients are already waiting for.

Nobody's saying hire a hygienist Day 1 of a startup when you don't have the patient base. But if you're booked out three weeks and still cleaning teeth yourself, the math is working against you and you're choosing it.

Marketing dependency, the leaky bucket.

You're spending $60–80K a year on marketing. You're getting 40–50 new patients a month. Sounds great. But your active patient count isn't going up.

We just reviewed a practice getting 257 new patients a year. 121 of them were not on the schedule for a second visit. That's $60K+ in lost annual patient value just sitting on the table. The bucket has a hole in it, and instead of patching it, you're just turning the hose up higher.

The leak is usually in the patient experience. Something between the first phone call and checkout is broken — wait times, no treatment plan ready at dismissal, weak reappointment language, personality friction, or just nobody actually asking the patient to come back. Everyone says "we always ask." Then we pull the KPIs and half the patients aren't rescheduled. Fix the bucket before you spend another dollar filling it.

You're house broke.

Your rent requires $2M in production to make sense and you're doing $1.2M. There's no efficiency hack for that. You need more volume — bring in a specialist or associate who adds procedures you don't do (implants, clear aligners, third molar extractions, sleep apnea), get marketing dialed in, and produce your way out. But go in with your eyes open: this isn't a systems problem, it's a fixed cost problem, and it only gets solved by growing into the space.

The associate you didn't need yet.

Around $1.2M is when you start thinking part-time associate. Some producers can stretch to $2M solo. But we see owners at $900K who already have an associate eating into their production because they wanted coverage for vacations or thought it would grow the practice. It doesn't work that way. If you're not large enough to support the associate's compensation without cannibalizing your own production, you just gave yourself a pay cut.

Your practice is profitable, but you're not managing your personal expenses.

Sometimes we do the analysis and the practice is fine. 45% profit, right in line with benchmarks. But the owner swears they're broke. Turns out they're maxing retirement vehicles, carrying lifestyle expenses, or both. That's not a practice problem. That's a household budget conversation.

Busy and profitable are two different problems. Figure out which one you actually have.
